name: Safety razor
lead: A safety razor is a razor in which a thin replaceable blade, usually double-edged, is clamped in a reusable handle behind a guard that limits how far the edge contacts the skin.[1] It succeeded the open straight razor and preceded modern multi-blade cartridges, and is favored by wet-shaving hobbyists, for example on forums such as Badger & Blade.[2][3]

Proponents say it gives a close shave with less irritation, fewer ingrown hairs and lower blade costs than cartridges. A 2024 near-infrared imaging study reportedly found less post-shave redness with a safety razor than a three-blade cartridge, but head-to-head trials on ingrown hairs are lacking and dermatology reviews stress technique and preparation over razor type.[4][5]

paras: The blade is clamped between a guard plate and a cap, with the edges partly enclosed so hair enters the narrow gap while the guard bar controls skin contact.[1] This differs from a straight razor, which has an exposed blade that needs honing, and from cartridge razors that integrate several blades in a disposable head.[1]

Grokipedia traces guarded razors to an 1847 design by William S. Henson and an 1880 patent by the Kampfe brothers, followed by King Camp Gillette's disposable double-edge blade, patented in 1904 and sold from 1903 at a price of $5 for a set.[1] Patent expiry in 1921 is said to have spurred competition.[1] These details come from an AI-generated source and are unverified here.

According to Grokipedia's summary, a multispectral near-infrared spectroscopy study of 59 men found less shaving-induced erythema with a safety razor than with a three-blade cartridge (40.3% versus 57.6% of skin areas).[1][4] That summary is the only description of the study that could be read here, and it concerns redness, not ingrown hairs.

Claims of fewer ingrown hairs are common in shaving communities and Grokipedia repeats them, but no independent controlled trial comparing razor types for ingrowns was found. A 2019 review of pseudofolliculitis barbae reports that multi-blade razors are commonly linked to the condition but notes a recent report blaming improper technique more than blade count.[5]

The 2019 review advises softening hair with warm water, avoiding stretching the skin, shaving against the grain and dry shaving, avoiding dull blades, and shaving often enough that hairs do not grow long.[5] Safety razors can still cut or nick the skin. A 1977 comparison for preoperative hair removal found that both razor and electric clipper damaged the skin surface, while a depilatory caused a mild reaction.[6] Case literature records razor use as a predisposing factor in axillary hidradenitis suppurativa.[7]
Wet-shaving forums host threads on beginners' setups, comparisons with electric shavers and shaving against the grain.[2][3][8]

One 2024 study of razor design and shaving-induced erythema compared razor types (see Effectiveness).[4] A 1977 comparative study examined razor, clipper and depilatory for surgical hair removal.[6] No trial was found comparing safety razors with cartridges for ingrown hairs.

timeline.event: William S. Henson designs a hoe-style guarded razor, per Grokipedia.[1]
Kampfe brothers patent the Star Safety Razor, per Grokipedia.[1]
Gillette granted a US patent for a razor with disposable double-edge blades, per Grokipedia.[1]
